title: Generating More Referrals
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article reframes the common sales advice to 'just ask for referrals' as often counterproductive, since most customers find premature referral requests off-putting. The author lays out a two-step sequence that must precede any ask: first, earn the referral through validated, exceptional work; second, refer the customer to something of value first, which triggers reciprocity. Only after both steps does asking (framed as a soft question rather than a direct request) become effective. The piece coins a memorable acronym, 'ERA' — earn, refer, ask — to summarize the sequence.
points: Asking directly for referrals is commonly recommended but often backfires, since most people find pre-emptive referral requests offensive or premature.
Before asking, performers must first earn the referral through validated, exceptional work and second refer the customer to something of value themselves.
Reciprocity drives referral behavior: people are more likely to refer someone who has already referred them to something worthwhile.
Framing the eventual ask as a question ('Is there someone who'd also benefit?') rather than a direct request reduces awkwardness for both parties.
quotes: The highest endorsement any performer can receive is to have an audience share the competence they’ve witnessed firsthand with those who trust them.
Most customers, audiences, and patrons find it offensive when performers ask for referrals before they are ready to give them.
The second step is less obvious. The performer must refer the audience, customer, or patron before they make a request. People are more likely to give referrals to those who refer them first.
By requesting the referral in the form of a question, those on the receiving end of this query don’t find it awkward, especially if they are not yet ready to endorse and refer.
Aside from baseball, a strong ERA stands for “earn, refer, and ask.” Make sure to do the first two steps before the ask.
